newsitem.title: USA: IBM seen exposing US stocks' vulnerability.
newsitem.headline: IBM seen exposing US stocks' vulnerability.

text.p: International Business Machines Corp's sharp opening sell-off highlights the precarious near-term position of many U.S. equities that have rallied fiercely despite warning signs that profit growth is slowing, analysts said.

The sentiment turnaround has not yet spilled over to the broad market and in fact, the technology-rich Nasdaq Composite and the Standard & Poor's 500 both posted mid-morning rises even as the Dow industrials tumbled 54 points to 6830, fully half of the dip coming from IBM's 9-1/8 point drop to 158-7/8.
Even so, warned analysts, the issues that have investors concerned over IBM apply directly to many companies and could foreshadow broader problems for equities down the road.
One particular factor is the strength of the dollar, which IBM said ate into fourth quarter revenue growth by three percentage points.

"The strong dollar is something I think is going to impact earnings for many multinationals," said Edgar Peters, chief investment strategist and director of asset allocation at PanAgora Asset Management Inc. "That's something that hasn't been talked about much before today."
The strong dollar hurts U.S. multinational companies in two ways. One is that profits from overseas are simply worth less when translated back into dollars.
They second strikes a blow at the companies' ability to compete, analysts said.

"It means the pricing power of domestic corporations is also hurt," said Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer and Co. "This foreshadows the real problem of 1997 because one of the pillars of this market has been earnings growth."

There is no indication the dollar is about to retreat. Modest profit-taking in early U.S. activity did pull the greenback down near 1.64 German marks and a trace below 119 yen, but those levels were still barely below multi-year highs against both currencies.
Likewise, there is little sign that companies are able to boost their pricing. While that keeps inflation in check, it may also threaten profit margins as average hourly wages continue to rise.
If worries about prices and inflation are mounting, it was not reflected in the bond market or the price of gold today.
The benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury was unchanged, yielding 6.79 percent and COMEX gold for February delivery fell $1.90 per ounce to $351.90.
